standfirst: A rookie lawyer with autism, a photographic memory and an unbroken interest in whales, walking into a firm with no idea what to do with her. What people actually loved was not the courtroom. It was that Woo Young-woo is never asked to become somebody else, and that Junho is patient in a way K-drama male leads rarely are. These six keep at least two of those three things.

picks.why: The first pick, and the closest one. Same shape: a legal procedural with a gentle, decent male lead and a female lead whose unusual ability is treated as a fact rather than a gimmick. Lee Jong-suk plays a prosecutor with the same unarmoured kindness. Difference: cases run two to four episodes instead of one, and there is a mild love triangle, handled far better than that phrase suggests.

The closest structural match almost nobody suggests. A savant lawyer, music instead of memory, a case-per-episode rhythm about people at their absolute worst, and one long grudge running underneath the whole thing. It even shares a cast member with Woo. Difference: no romance whatsoever. The central relationship is a three-man friendship, which is either a downgrade or the best trade on this list.

For the competence and the found family. A workplace where skilled adults are quietly good at their jobs and kinder to each other than the plot requires, with the same weekly rhythm of one case, one lesson, one small ache. Difference: no legal element and no single protagonist. Season one is the slice-of-life one; season two leans romance.

The other great K-drama with an autistic lead, and the better performance of the two if you can take the weight. Ten episodes of an uncle and nephew clearing the homes of people who died alone, built on genuine mutual dependence rather than protection. Difference: no romance and far heavier. Do not start it looking for comfort.

Park Eun-bin again, and the one to watch if what you actually loved was her. Fifteen years stranded, then a return to a world that moved on, played with the same mix of oddness and open-heartedness. Difference: it carries a domestic-abuse thread Woo never goes near, so it is a harder watch than the logline implies.

If the courtroom was the draw and you want the version with no softness in it. Ten episodic cases about children who did terrible things, argued out by adults who disagree honestly and are all partly right. Difference: the tone is the exact inverse. It is cold and built to leave you unsettled rather than reassured.

The right call if the real appeal was adults who say what they mean. Four characters, healthy communication, almost no manufactured conflict, and a second lead played by Kang Tae-oh, who was Junho. Difference: no cases and no plot engine. It is a hangout show and it moves like one.

against.title: Good Doctor
against.why: The reflex pick, because both leads are savants in a professional setting. But Good Doctor is a 2013 melodrama with a much more conventional idea of what a disabled protagonist is for. The 2022 sensibility that made Woo feel new is the exact thing missing.

against.title: It's Okay to Not Be Okay
against.why: Suggested because it also features an autistic character and a mental-health frame. That character is a supporting brother, though, and the show itself belongs to a violent, stylised romance. Nothing about the daily texture matches.

against.title: Taxi Driver
against.why: The other great episodic-justice show, and a different moral universe. It is a revenge fantasy where the answer is always violence. Woo's answer is always an argument. If what you liked was that the law worked, this will read as a different genre.
